READ_THIS_FIRST.what_was_wrong: The centrifugal term reinforced rather than opposed self-gravity, and the rotational part of the geopotential carried a sign inconsistent with the gravitational part.
READ_THIS_FIRST.how_it_was_found: Comparison with the analytic slope field of a uniformly rotating sphere (verification/rotsphere_check.py). A non-rotating sphere test cannot detect this error, because it returns zero slope for either sign.
READ_THIS_FIRST.effect: Mean slopes changed by -0.6 to -8.3 degrees depending on the body; the Ryugu per-facet correlation against the Hayabusa2 products improved from r=0.87 to r=0.9989 and the geopotential correlation from 0.38 to 0.9898.
READ_THIS_FIRST.terminology_note: Keys and notes written before the final manuscript revision use the phrase 'potential variance' for the quantity the paper now calls the NORMALIZED GEOPOTENTIAL DISPERSION. The quantity is unchanged: it is the area-weighted standard deviation of the surface geopotential divided by the absolute area-weighted mean, i.e. a coefficient of variation, not a variance. The wording was corrected in the manuscript; the JSON keys are left as they are so that earlier outputs remain traceable.
READ_THIS_FIRST.second_superseded_set: The key SUPERSEDED_paperV_conical_region_bug holds the first Paper V Itokawa inversion (6 Aug 2026). Its sub-regions were cones anchored at an interior point rather than plane-cut lobes, which reversed the sign of the recovered density contrast. It is retained for transparency and must NOT be used. The authoritative Paper V key is CORRECTED_paperV_plane_clipped_regions.

cross_shape_version_Itokawa.question: Can a ground-based (radar) shape substitute for a spacecraft-derived (Gaskell) shape?
cross_shape_version_Itokawa.finding: Bulk descriptors agree well: area-weighted slope average within 0.8%, potential variance within 7.9%. Distribution TAILS do not: the radar model has no facet above 41 deg and 1.7% above 30 deg, while the Gaskell model reaches 149 deg with 2.29% above 90 deg and 4.8% above 30 deg. Ground-based shapes therefore support bulk/global gravity descriptors but not local hazard or extreme-slope assessment.
cross_shape_version_Itokawa.IMPORTANT_correction: Our own radar-model run gives 13.40 deg (mean) / 14.75 deg (area-weighted), NOT the ~9 deg quoted in the literature for radar-based Itokawa. The Section 1 abstract claim of a near factor-of-two difference between shape versions under the same method is NOT supported by our computation and must be revised.

cross_shape_version_Kleopatra.status: CONFOUNDED - report with caveat or exclude
cross_shape_version_Kleopatra.caveat: The two Kleopatra models differ in SCALE, not only in surface detail: kleo.mod long axis is 276.3 km versus ~217 km for the Ostro model (+27%), while b and c axes are similar (aspect 2.9:1 vs 3.5:1). At fixed density the larger model has more mass and stronger gravity, reducing the relative centrifugal contribution and hence the slope. The 36-40% differences therefore conflate scale, aspect ratio and surface detail, and cannot be attributed to shape-model provenance. Itokawa (Gaskell vs radar, extents agreeing to 6-13%) is the clean cross-version test; Kleopatra is not.
cross_shape_version_Kleopatra.resolution_study_note: Both Kleopatra models saturate under decimation (4092 and 2292 facets); neither supports a proper resolution-convergence study. Recommend excluding Kleopatra from the resolution analysis.

bennu_density_sweep.agreement: Now QUANTITATIVE, not just trend: 25.55 vs ~24 at rho=0.85 (+1.5 deg); 16.06 vs ~15 at rho=1.15 (+1.1 deg); equatorial 11.19 vs ~12; polar 17.81 vs ~18. Pre-fix run gave 17.71 at rho=0.85, badly underestimating the published 24 deg.

smoothing_test.key_observation: Smoothing the spacecraft-derived Itokawa (Gaskell) model for 10 iterations gives 12.90 deg, close to the independent ground-based radar model value of 13.40 deg (3.7% apart). This supports the interpretation that the difference between the two shape versions is dominated by facet-scale roughness. For Eros the published ~11.5 deg lies between the unsmoothed (13.65) and heavily smoothed (10.30) values.

SUPERSEDED_paperV_conical_region_bug.what_was_wrong: Sub-regions were closed by fanning every boundary edge to an interior point O, giving faces (O, b, a). That mesh is watertight and its volume matches the tetrahedral sum to machine precision, but the solid it encloses is a CONE anchored at O, not the plane-cut lobe the density model intends. Raising the region density therefore added mass along a wedge reaching back to the centre of the body instead of adding it in the head or the neck slab.
SUPERSEDED_paperV_conical_region_bug.why_the_existing_check_missed_it: The reported 'volume closure error' compared the fan mesh against the sum of the same tetrahedra. Both quantities describe the cone, so the test verified internal consistency only and could never detect that the solid was the wrong one. Predicate testing (every vertex of the region must satisfy the defining inequality) is the check that discriminates.
SUPERSEDED_paperV_conical_region_bug.how_it_was_found: The inferred contrast reversed relative to the Paper IV pilot: the head came out LESS dense than the body, contradicting Kanamaru & Sasaki (2019). A unit-sphere control then showed the tetrahedral region reproducing the closed-form CONE volume and centroid rather than those of the spherical cap.

unit_sphere_diagnostic.geometry: unit sphere, O at centre, split plane x = 0.5

SUPERSEDED_paperV_conical_region_bug.note_on_the_paper4_pilot: The earlier pilot (paperV_density_estimation_pilot) was internally inconsistent in a related way: it evaluated the potential on a planar-capped head mesh but computed V_head as a sum of origin-anchored tetrahedra, i.e. a cone volume (0.0043996 of 0.017764 km^3, 24.8%). That mismatch is the likely origin of its '3% volume bias' note and of its monotonic head-model scan.

CORRECTED_paperV_plane_clipped_regions.method: Regions are built by exact plane clipping (Sutherland-Hodgman per triangle, intersection points snapped onto the plane, opening capped by fanning every boundary edge in reverse traversal to a coplanar apex). Total mass is held fixed, so each density model has one free parameter: rho_R * V_R + rho_rest * (V_tot - V_R) = M_total. The surface geopotential follows by superposition, U = rho_rest * U_full + (rho_R - rho_rest) * U_R, and the normalized geopotential dispersion is minimized over rho_R.

geometry_selftest_unit_sphere.note: Residuals near 0.1% are the polyhedral approximation of the sphere itself: the whole-body volume differs from 4*pi/3 by 0.05% at the same subdivision. The clipping is exact for the given polyhedron.

comparison_with_kanamaru_2019.note: Independent agreement: the two studies build the sub-region by different constructions and still recover the same sense and nearly the same magnitude of the head/body contrast.

detection_floor_assessment.verdict: The head-model signal (16.9%) lies well outside the Paper IV resolution band, whereas the neck-model signal (2.278%) lies inside it. At the conservative 5.9% noise level the neck density uncertainty (+/-819 kg/m^3) exceeds the recovered contrast itself (2525-1943 = 582 kg/m^3). On this body the head model, not the neck model, is the robust instrument - the opposite of the expectation carried into the run.

caveats: The head region (x > x_split) and the neck slab overlap, so the two models are not independent and must not be treated as such.
Absolute densities carry a systematic of about +3.3% from the shape model volume offset (see shape_model_volume_offset). The contrast is unaffected.

The automatic neck detector is mesh-dependent: it returned 0.1702 km on the two coarser meshes and 0.1608 km on the two finer ones. Any convergence claim must therefore hold the split plane fixed explicitly.

rho_head is not a split-invariant output. It varies by 38% across the sweep while the excess mass varies by 5%. Report the excess mass as the primary result and rho_head only alongside its split plane.
Dispersion minimization does not determine the split plane; it prefers ever smaller regions at ever higher densities. The plane must come from geomorphology plus the grain-density ceiling.
The LL-chondrite grain density used as the plausibility ceiling (3200 kg/m^3) is quoted from memory and must be verified against a current reference before publication.
itokawa.verdict: Both models yield an interior minimum and recover the head as the denser lobe, in agreement with Kanamaru & Sasaki (2019) and with the independent YORP spin-up evidence of Lowry et al. (2014). The inversion is stable under mesh refinement: two independent fixed-split pairs return identical densities. The head model carries a signal well outside the Paper IV resolution band; the neck model does not. The outstanding question is the sensitivity of the result to the choice of split plane.

mesh_convergence.design: Four meshes were run with the split plane left to automatic neck detection. The detector returned x = 0.1702 km on the two coarser meshes and x = 0.1608 km on the two finer ones, which turns the series into a 2x2: two independent pairs that each hold the split plane fixed while the facet count changes.

pair_B_fixed_split_0p1608.note: 49152 is the unreduced model; no decimation was applied.

split_plane_sensitivity.caveat: Estimated from two split positions only, and the two positions also differ in mesh. A single-mesh sweep over x_split is required before quoting these slopes.
split_plane_sensitivity.SUPERSEDED_BY: split_plane_sweep. The two-point estimate of 10.6 kg/m^3 per metre holds only near the neck; the sweep gives 7.5 over 0.130 to 0.160 km and up to 55 by 0.240 km.

mesh_convergence.conclusion: The density recovered by the inversion is invariant under mesh refinement to the resolution of the density scan (25 kg/m^3): both fixed-split pairs return identical rho_head, rho_rest and rho_neck. Paper IV established that the geopotential dispersion converges under refinement; this establishes the separate and stronger property that the density inferred by minimizing it converges as well. The dominant uncertainty in the inversion is therefore not mesh resolution but the choice of the split plane.

shape_model_volume_offset.CORRECTION: An earlier entry in this file attributed the difference between the bulk density computed here (about 2013 kg/m^3) and the published value (about 1950 kg/m^3) to volume loss during decimation. That attribution was WRONG and has been removed. It was refuted by the 49152-facet run, which applies no decimation at all and returns essentially the same volume as the decimated meshes.
shape_model_volume_offset.actual_cause: The shape model itself encloses less volume than the published figure. This file's model gives 0.0177856 km^3 against a published Itokawa volume of about 0.01840 km^3, i.e. 3.34% smaller. With the total mass of 3.58e10 kg, the published volume yields 1946 kg/m^3, matching the literature value, while the model volume yields 2012.9 kg/m^3.
shape_model_volume_offset.consequence: All absolute densities reported here are inflated by about 3.3% relative to what the published volume would give, at fixed total mass. This is a systematic of the shape model and its scaling, not a numerical artefact, and cannot be removed by refining the mesh. The contrast rho_R/rho_rest is a ratio and is unaffected.

CORRECTION_naive_rescaling_is_invalid.what_was_recorded_before: rho_head_rescaled_to_published_volume = 2708 and rho_rest_rescaled_to_published_volume = 1797, obtained by multiplying the recovered densities by the ratio of the published bulk density to ours.
CORRECTION_naive_rescaling_is_invalid.why_it_is_wrong: Enlarging the body to the published volume at fixed mass does not simply divide every density by the volume ratio, because gravity and the centrifugal term do not scale together. Gravity goes as GM/L^2 and falls when the body is enlarged at fixed mass; the centrifugal term goes as omega^2 L and rises. Their ratio therefore changes, the shape of the surface geopotential changes with it, and the density the inversion prefers is not the old one times a constant. This is the same mechanism that reverses the sign of the Arrokoth contrast when the assumed mass is varied.
CORRECTION_naive_rescaling_is_invalid.status: the rescaled values are withdrawn; see scale_test for a measured answer

what_the_offset_does_and_does_not_affect.contrast: UNAFFECTED. It is a ratio, so a common factor on both densities cancels.
what_the_offset_does_and_does_not_affect.excess_mass: UNAFFECTED to first order. If the true body is larger by a factor s in volume then V_R grows by s while the densities fall by s at fixed total mass, and dM = drho * V_R is the product of the two. The cancellation is exact only in the scaling argument; the measured answer is in scale_test.
what_the_offset_does_and_does_not_affect.absolute_densities: AFFECTED. They are inflated by about 3.3% because the model volume is that much smaller than the published figure.
what_the_offset_does_and_does_not_affect.reporting_decision: Report all three. The contrast and the excess mass are the primary results and carry a note that they are insensitive to the offset. Absolute densities are reported as computed, always together with the volume and bulk density they rest on, and never as a naively rescaled number.

scale_test.method: The Itokawa mesh was enlarged by a linear factor of 1.011385, the cube root of 0.01840/0.0177856, bringing its volume to the published figure at fixed total mass. The split plane was moved with it, from 0.1608 to 0.1627 km, so that the same physical surface is cut; using the same numerical value would have compared two different planes in body-relative terms.

configuration.note: the region fraction is preserved to 0.06%, confirming the plane was moved correctly

scale_test.CONCLUSION: The contrast and the excess mass are confirmed insensitive to the volume offset: they move by 0.32% and 0.92%, against a scan resolution of 0.89% and sweep variations of 13% and 5%. Absolute densities move by the expected 3.3%. All three can therefore be reported, with the first two as the primary results.
scale_test.REVISION_of_the_earlier_warning: An earlier entry called the naively rescaled values 2708 and 1797 'wrong'. That was too strong. The REASONING was invalid - gravity and the centrifugal term do not scale together, so a common factor is not guaranteed - but the numbers turn out to be accurate: the measurement gives 2700 and 1797, the naive prediction 2706.5 and 1796.0, both within one 25 kg/m^3 scan step. The reason is that Itokawa rotates slowly enough that the centrifugal term is only 3.68% of the surface acceleration, rising to 3.81% after the enlargement, so the balance barely shifts. This is a measured property of this body, not a general licence: on a faster rotator, or where the centrifugal term is a larger share, naive rescaling would fail. Arrokoth is the demonstration, where changing the assumed mass reverses the sign of the contrast outright.

invariance_analysis.conclusion: The excess mass in the head is by far the most split-invariant quantity the inversion returns: it varies by about 5% across the whole sweep, against 38% for rho_head and for the contrast. As the plane advances the region shrinks and rho_head rises in near compensation, holding the product almost fixed. What potential-dispersion minimization actually constrains is therefore the excess MASS of the head, not its density. rho_head is a derived quantity and is only meaningful when quoted together with the split plane that produced it.
invariance_analysis.MECHANISM_CONFIRMED: See synthetic_invariance_test. The invariance of the excess mass is the signature of a detectable mass anomaly, not a property of the method. In a controlled synthetic family the scaling slope moves toward -1 as the signal strengthens (correlation 0.95), and bodies with no anomaly show a density difference that changes sign, so nothing is invariant. This explains why Itokawa behaves as it does and 67P and Arrokoth do not.

physical_plausibility_limit.basis: Itokawa is an LL-chondrite body (LL5/LL6). The grain density of LL-chondrite material is the zero-porosity ceiling: no region of the body can be denser than the mineral matrix itself.
physical_plausibility_limit.VERIFY_BEFORE_PUBLICATION: The value 3200 kg/m^3 is taken from memory of the LL-chondrite meteorite literature and must be checked against a current reference before it is quoted. A looser ceiling of 3300 would shift the limit slightly.
physical_plausibility_limit.implied_constraint: The split plane must lie at x <= about 0.19 km, otherwise the inferred head density exceeds the zero-porosity ceiling for LL-chondrite material.

crossing_bracket.note: Bracketed by runs 5 m apart; the 25 kg/m^3 scan step puts about +/-0.0013 km of quantisation on the crossing.

physical_plausibility_limit.relation_to_the_neck: The neck slab's upper edge is at 0.2029 km. The bound of 0.2069 km lies 4.0 m beyond it, but the lower end of its range, 0.2022 km, coincides with the edge to 0.7 m. Geomorphology and the grain-density ceiling agree within the uncertainty of the latter.
physical_plausibility_limit.note_on_the_earlier_value: The earlier bound of 0.1925 km was computed with a ceiling of 3200 kg/m^3, which is the LL BULK density, not the grain density.

retracted_hypothesis_joint_minimum.hypothesis: That the dispersion at the minimum would itself turn around as a function of x_split, yielding a joint minimum in (rho_head, x_split) and so determining the split plane from the data alone.

evidence.extrapolated_turning_point_km: 0.244 to 0.259 (cubic and quartic fits to the last points)

retracted_hypothesis_joint_minimum.why_retracted: The extrapolated turning point lies at splits where the required head density is 5000 kg/m^3 or more, far above the LL-chondrite grain density. The turning point is therefore mathematical only and sits entirely inside the physically meaningless region. Dispersion minimization alone does not fix the split plane: it always prefers a smaller region with a higher density, because what it holds fixed is the excess mass. The plane must be set from outside the method, by the geomorphology of the neck together with the grain-density ceiling.

well_curvature_vs_region_size.illustration: At x_split = 0.220 the dispersion at rho_head = 3700 and at 4125 differs by 4e-6, while the densities differ by 425 kg/m^3.
well_curvature_vs_region_size.practical_floor: A region below roughly 10 to 15% of the body volume no longer constrains its own density usefully, only its excess mass.

eros_negative_control.STATUS: AUTHORITATIVE - negative control for Paper V
eros_negative_control.purpose: Eros is believed to be close to uniform in density, and it is not a contact binary. If potential-dispersion minimization manufactured a contrast out of shape asymmetry alone, this is where it would show: Eros is long, irregular, carries a pronounced saddle, and rotates more than twice as fast as Itokawa.

neck_detector_failure.diagnosis: find_neck() trims the ends and then takes the ABSOLUTE minimum of the binned cross-section profile inside the remaining window. On Itokawa the neck is the absolute minimum, so this works. Eros tapers at both ends, so the smallest half-width inside the window falls on the shoulder at x = -10.76 km (5.25 km) rather than in the genuine saddle at x = +4.47 km (6.08 km), which is a LOCAL minimum between the two humps at -2.60 km (8.35 km) and +10.45 km (7.94 km).
neck_detector_failure.consequence: The detector fails silently on bodies that are not contact binaries: it returns a plausible-looking number that is not a saddle at all. It should locate a true local minimum, and should report when none exists.
neck_detector_failure.action_taken: x_split was set explicitly to 4.47 km (Himeros).

comparison_with_itokawa.itokawa_reference: head model at the matched split x = 0.150 km

verdict.passes_when: The split plane is placed at the true saddle. At x = 4.47 km the signal is 0.417%, below even the 0.60% plateau bound from Paper IV and indistinguishable from zero, and the contrast of 1.018 lies inside the 1.000 +/- 0.019 band set by the curvature of the minimum.
verdict.fails_when: The plane is misplaced. At the detector's choice of x = -10.7619 km the same uniform body returns contrast 0.875 and an improvement of 5.539%, thirteen times larger, with a centre-of-mass offset four times larger and of opposite sign.
verdict.revised_conclusion: Potential-dispersion minimization does not manufacture a density contrast from shape asymmetry alone PROVIDED the split plane is correctly placed. Correct placement is a precondition of the method, not a detail of its implementation. The Itokawa signal of 16.9% remains far above anything misplacement produced here, so it stands; but the earlier unqualified statement that the method cannot generate spurious contrast was too strong and is superseded by this entry.
verdict.why_this_is_a_strong_test: The Eros region at the true saddle is 34.6% of the body against 17.9% for Itokawa, so it is better constrained, not worse: the uncertainty on its density is +/-51 kg/m^3 against +/-130 for Itokawa. The null result is a genuine absence of contrast rather than an inability to resolve one.

head_model_at_detector_position.purpose: Quantify how much apparent structure a misplaced split plane creates on a body with no real contrast. This is the position the automatic neck detector chose, so it is what a default run would produce.

apparent_well_sharpness_is_an_artefact.why_misleading: With the complement holding only 11.6% of the volume, the mass constraint forces rho_complement to swing violently for small changes in rho_region: 19263 at rho_region = 500, 3957 at 2500, 131 at 3000. Nearly all of that range is physically impossible. The dispersion therefore rises steeply on both sides of the minimum and the well looks sharply defined, but the sharpness comes from the constraint amplification, not from information about the density.

spurious_signal_from_misplacement.significance: The misplaced-plane signal of 5.539% sits just inside the upper bound of the Paper IV noise band (0.9 to 5.9%), so it is not formally significant. But it is thirteen times the correctly placed value and would readily be mistaken for a genuine weak contrast on a body believed to be uniform.
spurious_signal_from_misplacement.compounding_hazard: The automatic detector selects this very position and gives no warning. A default run on Eros therefore returns contrast 0.875 with an improvement of 5.5% and nothing to indicate the result is meaningless.

neck_detector_fix.problem: find_neck trimmed the ends of the binned cross-section profile and returned the ABSOLUTE minimum of what remained. A neck is a local minimum with a hump on either side; the smallest interior half-width of a body that tapers at both ends lies on a flank instead. The routine therefore failed silently on Eros, returning a plausible number that was not a saddle, and that position produced a spurious contrast of 0.875 on a body with none.
neck_detector_fix.fix: Candidates are now local minima detected on RUNS of equal profile value rather than on single points, each accepted only if it has a strictly higher value on both sides. Prominence is measured against the lower of the two flanking humps, normalised by the largest half-width, and a candidate must reach min_prominence = 0.02. The most prominent candidate is selected. If none qualifies the routine returns None and the caller must supply --xsplit; the neck model is skipped rather than run on a guess. Whenever the selected saddle differs from the absolute interior minimum, the run prints a NOTE naming the rejected position.
neck_detector_fix.run_detection_was_necessary: A first version tested single points with strict inequalities and REJECTED Itokawa outright: the profile is nearly symmetric about the neck, so the two samples either side of the minimum carry equal values and neither is strictly below its neighbours. Run-based detection also handles plateaux. This regression was caught by the synthetic test set before the change reached the real data.

sliver_warning_test.why_it_was_not_assumed_harmless: The contribution of a sliver is proportional to its area and should vanish, but catastrophic cancellation could in principle make it large instead: the coordinates are of order 1700 m while the triangle is 2 mm across, a ratio near the limit of double precision. Three earlier bugs in this project all produced plausible-looking numbers, so the question was settled by measurement rather than argument.
sliver_warning_test.test: The 67P reference run was repeated with --cliptol 1e-6, i.e. 5.5 mm for this body, which snaps the offending vertices onto the plane. Everything else was identical.

excess_mass_invariance_DOES_NOT_GENERALI.earlier_claim: That what potential-dispersion minimization constrains is the excess mass of the region rather than its density, stated as a property of the method.
excess_mass_invariance_DOES_NOT_GENERALI.test: Repeat the Itokawa split-plane sweep on 67P and on Arrokoth and ask, on each body, which of rho_head and the excess mass varies less.
excess_mass_invariance_DOES_NOT_GENERALI.finding: On the two new bodies the excess mass varies about ten times MORE than the density, the reverse of Itokawa.
excess_mass_invariance_DOES_NOT_GENERALI.explanation: The compensation that keeps the excess mass fixed on Itokawa is the signature of fitting a real mass anomaly: as the plane advances the region shrinks and rho_head rises almost exactly in step, holding the product constant. Where there is no anomaly, rho_R simply sits near the bulk value and the excess mass, being a small residual times V_R, tracks the region volume instead. The invariance is therefore a property of a body with a detectable anomaly, not of the method.
excess_mass_invariance_DOES_NOT_GENERALI.narrowed_claim: WHERE the method detects a signal above the noise band, what it constrains is the excess mass rather than the density. synthetic_invariance_test.STATUS: AUTHORITATIVE - supports the mechanism, with stated limits
synthetic_invariance_test.question: The excess mass was the steadier quantity on Itokawa and the less steady one on 67P and Arrokoth. Is that because the invariance is the signature of a real mass anomaly rather than a property of the method?
synthetic_invariance_test.why_not_another_real_body: We cannot choose in advance whether a further body will carry a signal, and no body's true interior is known, so agreement would only establish that it happened twice. A synthetic family lets the signal strength be varied while everything else is controlled.
synthetic_invariance_test.what_is_NOT_tested: Recovery of an imposed density. Potential-dispersion minimization does not fit observations: it assumes the true density is the one that flattens the surface geopotential. Imposing an arbitrary density and asking for it back would fail by construction and would test nothing. What is tested is the structure of the objective function.

design.bodies: Unions of prolate lobes of revolution about x, meshed directly. Eight bodies in three groups: a near-spherical control; a symmetric family with equal lobes, which is symmetric about its neck and so should prefer a contrast of 1; and an asymmetric family with unequal lobes, which has a genuine mass asymmetry to find.
design.plane_selection: Planes are chosen by bisection on the fraction of volume they leave above them, spanning a factor 1.90 in region volume centred on the fraction at the neck. This matches the Itokawa sweep, so bodies are compared over the same relative change of region size rather than the same distance in kilometres.
design.first_attempt_was_flawed: The first version swept a fixed +/-0.05 km on every body, which changed the region volume by only 1.13 to 1.54 against Itokawa's 1.90, so the comparison was not like for like. It also reported the half range of the excess mass as a percentage of its mean, which explodes when the mean sits inside the spread; the symmetric bodies produced apparent ratios of 252 to 1623 that were entirely artefacts of dividing by nearly zero. Both were corrected.

primary_diagnostic.definition: The slope of log(rho_R - rho_rest) against log(V_R). Since the excess mass is dM = drho * V_R, a slope of -1 means dM is held fixed as the plane moves and a slope of 0 means the density difference is held fixed instead.
primary_diagnostic.advantage: It does not break down when dM approaches zero. Where the density difference changes sign it simply returns nothing, which is the correct answer: there is no anomaly to hold fixed.

three_regimes.behaviour: The density difference changes sign across the sweep. Neither quantity is invariant because neither has anything to be invariant about.
The density is the steadier quantity, by a factor 3 to 4.
The excess mass becomes the steadier quantity.

correlation_signal_vs_slope.meaning: Positive means the slope rises toward -1 as the signal strengthens, which is what the proposed mechanism predicts.

comparison_with_itokawa.assessment: The only synthetic body that reproduces Itokawa's behaviour is the one carrying the strongest signal, and it reproduces it closely on all four measures.

LIMITS_OF_THIS_EVIDENCE: Only four bodies carry an anomaly, and three of them cluster between 16.7 and 19.5% improvement while the fourth sits at 43.7%. The correlation of 0.95 therefore rests on a single high-leverage point. The DIRECTION of the effect is supported; its functional form is not determined, and the data are equally consistent with a threshold somewhere between 20 and 44%.

The numerical threshold does not transfer. The synthetic bodies need about 44% improvement to reach excess-mass invariance while Itokawa reaches it at 26.4%. The synthetic bodies are smooth surfaces of revolution; real bodies carry roughness, which Paper IV found contributes an error floor of order two percentage points. No threshold value should be quoted as universal.

The test uses the same forward model in both directions, so it examines the structure of the objective function rather than the accuracy of the forward model. That accuracy was established separately in Paper IV against the JAXA Ryugu field (r = 0.9989).

sliver_control.why: The bisection places planes arbitrarily close to vertex rings of the mesh, producing many more sliver triangles than the 67P runs did, with vertices separated by about 2e-7 m. The earlier test was on one body at one plane and should not be assumed to carry over.

arrokoth_refined.STATUS: AUTHORITATIVE - supersedes the position-based Arrokoth sweep
arrokoth_refined.why_redone: The first Arrokoth sweep chose planes by position, from x = -6.5 to -3.0 km. Planes are now chosen by bisection on the volume fraction, spanning a factor 1.89 to match Itokawa and the synthetic family.

part_A_sweep_by_volume_fraction.bisection_accuracy: every plane hit its target fraction to four decimal places
part_A_sweep_by_volume_fraction.KEY_RESULT: At a region fraction of 61.2% the inversion returns the uniform solution exactly: rho_R = rho_rest = 400 kg/m^3, contrast 1.0000, improvement -0.000%. The density difference changes sign about that point, running from +33.3 to -61.5 kg/m^3 across the sweep, so the scaling slope does not exist. Arrokoth therefore belongs in the no-anomaly regime alongside the sphere and the symmetric synthetic family, and can now be placed in the central figure rather than omitted.
part_A_sweep_by_volume_fraction.improvement_note: The improvement rises away from the null in both directions, reaching 5.35% at the largest region. That is still inside the Paper IV band of 0.9 to 5.9%, and it is the expected behaviour when a two-region model is fitted to a body that has no anomaly: the further the plane sits from the null, the more apparent improvement can be extracted from noise.

part_B_mesh_convergence.purpose: The claim that the inferred density converges under mesh refinement rested on Itokawa alone, the same single-body weakness the excess-mass claim turned out to have. These runs hold the plane fixed at the neck, x = -4.7863 km, and vary the facet count.
part_B_mesh_convergence.why_xsplit_and_not_fracsplit: A convergence test must hold the plane itself fixed. Selecting by fraction would let the plane move with the mesh and the two effects could not be separated - the same confound that made the first Itokawa mesh series a 2x2 by accident.

after_normalising_by_bulk_density.note: Part of the 5 kg/m^3 shift is not the inversion at all but the volume the coarse mesh loses, which raises the bulk density it is measured against.

derived_quantities_are_less_converged.explanation: The contrast and the excess mass are small residuals on a body with no anomaly, so in relative terms they move a great deal while the densities themselves barely move. All three values remain consistent with zero.

RESTATED_overlap_caveat.old_wording: The head region (x > x_split) and the neck slab overlap, so the two models are not independent and must not be treated as such.
RESTATED_overlap_caveat.why_it_needed_restating: The old wording implied two competing detections whose independence mattered. There is only one detection in the whole study, and it comes from the head model on Itokawa. The neck model contributes no detection anywhere, so the question of independence between two positive results does not arise.

THE_PLATEAU_EXPLAINS_WHY_OUR_INFERENCE_S.observation: On Itokawa the global curve is flat above about 1000 kg/m^3. The minimum they find at 330 sits on the falling left flank, where rotation finally becomes comparable to gravity.
THE_PLATEAU_EXPLAINS_WHY_OUR_INFERENCE_S.why: The normalised dispersion is sd(U_grav + U_rot) / |mean(U_grav + U_rot)|. The gravitational part scales linearly with the assumed bulk density while the rotational part does not. Once rotation is negligible the density cancels between numerator and denominator and the normalised dispersion becomes INDEPENDENT of the bulk density. That is the plateau.
THE_PLATEAU_EXPLAINS_WHY_OUR_INFERENCE_S.consequence_for_bulk_density_inference: On a slow rotator the plateau carries no information about the bulk density, so the minimisation is pushed onto the flank and returns an absurdly low value. This is exactly what happens to Itokawa at 330 against a measured 1950, and it is what their first criterion is guarding against.
THE_PLATEAU_EXPLAINS_WHY_OUR_INFERENCE_S.consequence_for_THIS_work: Varying the INTERIOR distribution at fixed total mass is a different operation. It does not rescale the field; it changes the shape of U_grav across the surface, which changes the ratio of its standard deviation to its mean. The information that the plateau destroys for the bulk-density problem is therefore still present for the distribution problem. This is a physical argument, derived from their own figure, for why the inference here survives on a body that fails their first criterion.

Richardson_2019_READ.ref: Richardson J. E., Graves K. J., Harris A. W. & Bowling T. J. (2019), Icarus 329, 207-221
Richardson_2019_READ.content: A geomorphological examination of 32 small-body shape models with their spin properties, showing that shape, gravity and spin drive surfaces toward a state of maximum topographic stability. 15 of the 32 lie within that zone, and when lightcurve-derived rotation rates and elongations are included, 1941 of 2791 well-observed asteroids do.
Richardson_2019_READ.their_ratio_definition: U_rot / U_grav = omega^2 / (4 pi G rho) for a perfect sphere; the tabulated values use the real shape, so the sphere formula does not reproduce them. Richardson_2019_READ.relevance_to_a_follow_up: This is a survey of topographic stability and bulk density across many bodies, not of interior contrast. A follow-up applying the two-region contrast method to radar shapes would not duplicate it, but the overlap in data and framing is real and the survey must be cited and distinguished carefully.

THE_3190_QUESTION_IS_SETTLED.Fujiwara_verbatim: 'a typical value for their BULK DENSITY is 3.2 g cm^-3, the macroporosity of Itokawa is estimated to be about 41%'

THE_3190_QUESTION_IS_SETTLED.VERDICT: Both Science papers call 3.19-3.2 g/cm^3 the BULK density of LL chondrites. Kanamaru's label of grain density is a misattribution of their own cited source. The value is consistent with Consolmagno et al. (2008), who give 3.22 +/- 0.22 for the LL bulk density and 3.54 +/- 0.13 for the LL grain density. There is no disagreement in the measurements, only in the label.
THE_3190_QUESTION_IS_SETTLED.consequence_for_this_work: Our first use of about 3200 as the ceiling was correct in substance: it is the density of intact chondritic material, the right bound for an aggregate of such blocks. The later 'correction' to 3540 was an over-reach in one direction, and the still later suggestion that Kanamaru's usage settled the matter was an over-reach in the other. The settled position: report the bound under both, 3220 for a pile of intact blocks and 3540 for the absolute mineral limit, and note in passing that the Itokawa literature has propagated the grain-density label for what its own sources call a bulk density.
THE_3190_QUESTION_IS_SETTLED.porosity_arithmetic: Abe's 40% and Fujiwara's 41% both follow from 1950/3190 = 0.61, so the porosity figures in the Itokawa literature are macroporosities relative to meteorite bulk density, as they should be.

MASS_AND_VOLUME_AS_PUBLISHED.note_on_the_two_masses: The two papers appeared in the same issue of Science and give 3.58e10 and 3.51e10 kg. Abe's is the dedicated mass determination from descent tracking; Fujiwara's earlier figure is described in that paper as having suffered from errors. This work uses 3.58e10, which is defensible, but the 2% difference should be acknowledged.

THE_VOLUME_OFFSET_IS_NOT_SIGNIFICANT.REVISION: The volume offset has been treated throughout this work as a systematic to be flagged. In fact it sits well inside the published uncertainty on the volume, which is 5%. It is not evidence that the shape model is wrong; it is an ordinary difference between one shape model and the figure adopted in 2006. Report it as such, and stop describing it as an offset that inflates the densities: the published density itself is uncertain at 7% and our value is within half a sigma of it.
THE_VOLUME_OFFSET_IS_NOT_SIGNIFICANT.what_still_holds: The scale test remains useful: it shows that contrast and excess mass move by less than 1% when the volume is changed to the published figure, so the primary results do not depend on which is adopted.

Tatsumi_Sugita_2018_READ.ref: Tatsumi E. & Sugita S. (2018), Icarus 300, 227-248, 'Cratering efficiency on coarse-grain targets: implications for the dynamical evolution of asteroid 25143 Itokawa'
Tatsumi_Sugita_2018_READ.relevance: It bears on Richardson & Bowling's third and fourth conditions, which this work has so far been unable to assess for Itokawa.
Tatsumi_Sugita_2018_READ.condition_3_a_disturbance_source: Impact-induced seismic shaking is active on Itokawa: they invoke it to explain the depletion of small quasi-circular depressions, noting that 'seismic shaking would obliterate smaller quasi-circular depressions efficiently', and cite regolith convection and migration as further obliteration processes. Condition 3 is plausibly satisfied.
Tatsumi_Sugita_2018_READ.condition_4_time_since_resurfacing: The crater retention age is 3-33 Myr in the main belt, in agreement with cosmic-ray exposure ages of the returned samples, and they conclude that a global resurfacing resetting the top 1-10 m occurred long after the disruption of the parent body at about 1.3 Gyr. Condition 4 is plausibly satisfied.
Tatsumi_Sugita_2018_READ.net_assessment_of_the_four_conditions_fo: Condition 1, a significant rotational force, is the one Richardson & Bowling say Itokawa fails, at a potential ratio of 0.024. Condition 2, mobile regolith, is supported by the Muses Sea and the smooth terrains that cover about 20% of the surface. Conditions 3 and 4 are supported by Tatsumi & Sugita. So Itokawa satisfies three of the four, and fails only on rotation. That is a more precise and more defensible statement than the blanket claim that the premise is weak on this body.

Scheeres_Gaskell_2008_READ_IN_FULL.ref: Scheeres D. J. & Gaskell R. W. (2008), Effect of density inhomogeneity on YORP: the case of Itokawa, Icarus 198, 125-129, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2008.07.010
Scheeres_Gaskell_2008_READ_IN_FULL.MY_EARLIER_DESCRIPTION_WAS_WRONG: I told the user twice that the title was The dynamical evolution of asteroid 25143 Itokawa, and described the paper as the origin of the argument that a centre-of-mass offset toward the HEAD implies a denser head. Both were wrong. The title is Effect of density inhomogeneity on YORP, and the paper argues for a density concentration in the NECK. This is the fifth error made from memory in this project.
Scheeres_Gaskell_2008_READ_IN_FULL.what_they_actually_do: They show that a density inhomogeneity offsets the centre of mass from the centre of figure and reorients the principal axes, both of which alter the predicted YORP rate. Applying this to Itokawa they find the YORP angular velocity rate is sensitive to the offset: a few metres changes the deceleration significantly and 10 to 15 metres can change its SIGN, making the spin rate accelerate. The smallest shift giving zero YORP is 16 m for the 0.5 m resolution shape model and under 9 m for the 4 m model.
Scheeres_Gaskell_2008_READ_IN_FULL.their_conclusion_VERBATIM: The current non-detection of YORP for Itokawa is consistent with a density concentration in the neck region of Itokawa.
Scheeres_Gaskell_2008_READ_IN_FULL.their_physical_argument: Loose regolith has migrated into the neck from higher elevations while the rest of the surface is rocky and devoid of finer regolith. Assuming a common grain density for all the material, the neck would then have a higher bulk density than its surroundings, shifting the centre of mass toward the neck.

THE_HEAD_VERSUS_NECK_QUESTION_IS_OLDER_T.why_the_ambiguity_persists: The neck sits at x = +150 m while the centre of figure is near x = 0, so a shift toward the neck and a shift toward the head are both in the +x direction. A centre-of-mass offset alone cannot separate the two hypotheses, and it has not separated them since 2008.
THE_HEAD_VERSUS_NECK_QUESTION_IS_OLDER_T.a_prediction_that_came_true: Scheeres & Gaskell wrote that a dense neck could give Itokawa a positive rotation rate. Lowry et al. subsequently measured a spin-up. The direction was predicted correctly while the structural interpretation remained open.

CONSEQUENCES_FOR_PAPER_V: Restore Scheeres & Gaskell (2008) to the bibliography with the correct title.
Do NOT attribute the dense-head interpretation to them. They argue for a dense neck.

Section 3.5 should present the head-versus-neck question as a thread running from 2008 to the present rather than as a remark made by Kanamaru in 2019. This strengthens the case for reporting the degeneracy honestly: it is not a minor caveat but an eighteen-year-old open question.

The neck model of this work acquires more context: it is the parameterisation Scheeres & Gaskell and Kanamaru both favour, and it yields no detection here, with an uncertainty of 10.3% of the recovered value on Itokawa. That is worth stating plainly.

mass_sensitivity_test_Itokawa.design: Five runs on the identical Itokawa mesh, 49152 facets, volume 0.0177856 km^3, plane fixed at x = 0.1608 km. The only thing varied is the assumed total mass, over a factor of four. The scale test could not do this cleanly because it enlarged the mesh at the same time.

PLATEAU_ARGUMENT_RETRACTED.what_was_claimed: That the normalised dispersion becomes independent of the assumed bulk density once rotation is negligible, so that Richardson & Bowling's bulk-density inference has no information to work with on Itokawa while our interior inference still does.
PLATEAU_ARGUMENT_RETRACTED.what_the_measurement_shows: The dispersion rises monotonically from 0.06957 at 1006 kg/m^3 to 0.09559 at 4026, a rise of 37.4% over a factor of four, with a log-log slope of +0.224. A plateau would give a slope of zero. Itokawa at its true density is NOT on the plateau.
PLATEAU_ARGUMENT_RETRACTED.why_the_argument_failed: The limit itself is real: as rho grows without bound the density cancels between numerator and denominator and the ratio tends to sd(u)/|mean(u)|. The error was assuming Itokawa is in that limit because the rotational term is only 2.4% of the mean potential. A term can be negligible in the MEAN and dominant in the SPREAD. The rotational potential varies as the square of the distance from the spin axis, from zero at the poles to a maximum at the equator, while the gravitational potential is comparatively uniform - which is the premise of the whole method. So U_rot contributes little to the mean and a great deal to the dispersion.
PLATEAU_ARGUMENT_RETRACTED.lesson: The same mistake in miniature as the earlier ones: a plausible argument asserted before it was measured. It took one batch of five runs to settle.

A_BETTER_CROSS_CHECK_WITH_RICHARDSON_BOW.method: Extrapolate our five points linearly in 1/rho to the rho -> infinity asymptote, which is the quantity their plateau represents.
A_BETTER_CROSS_CHECK_WITH_RICHARDSON_BOW.assessment: This is a far better comparison than setting our 0.0866 at the true density against their plateau, because the two are different points on the same curve. The asymptotes agree. Our curve at 2013 kg/m^3 sits below the asymptote because rotation still contributes, exactly as their figure shows the global curve still climbing in that range.

THE_RESULT_THAT_MATTERS.finding: A FOURFOLD change in the assumed total mass moves the recovered contrast by only 11.0%, from 1.404 to 1.569, and never brings it near unity. The improvement moves by 4.5%, from 16.30% to 17.05%.
THE_RESULT_THAT_MATTERS.comparison_with_Arrokoth: On Arrokoth, doubling the assumed density from 250 to 500 reversed the sign of the contrast outright, from 1.062 to 0.916, with the crossing at about 339 kg/m^3.
THE_RESULT_THAT_MATTERS.NEW_DIAGNOSTIC: Sensitivity to the assumed mass is itself a signal diagnostic. Where a real contrast exists the inference is robust to the mass assumption; where it does not, the sign of the answer is set by that assumption rather than by the data. This is a second, independent way of distinguishing a detection from a null, and it does not require a split-plane sweep.
THE_RESULT_THAT_MATTERS.consequence_for_the_Itokawa_result: The one detection in this study does not depend on the measured mass being right to better than a factor of a few. That is worth stating, because the Itokawa shape model carries a 3.34% volume offset and the bulk density is uncertain at the 7% level.

mass_sensitivity_test_Itokawa.what_still_stands_from_the_earlier_discu: Richardson & Bowling's global minimisation on Itokawa returns 330 kg/m^3 against a measured 1950, and they attribute it to the body failing their first condition. That remains true and is their own statement. What must be dropped is our explanation of WHY the interior inference survives it. The honest replacement is empirical: the interior inference is measured to be insensitive to the assumed mass over a factor of four, while the bulk-density inference is not, and the reason is that the two problems move in different directions in parameter space.

manifold_defect_found_and_fixed.THE_DEFECT: Intersection points were created once per FACET rather than once per EDGE. The two facets sharing a cut edge therefore referenced two distinct vertex indices at the same position, and the clipped surface was torn along the entire cut. On a synthetic bilobe the region mesh had 432 unmatched directed edges and an Euler characteristic of 25 instead of 2; every cap-loop vertex had degree 1.
manifold_defect_found_and_fixed.why_no_test_caught_it: The divergence-theorem volume is a sum of signed tetrahedra and requires only that the oriented facets tile the boundary with correct signs, not that they are stitched together. The analytic comparison, the complement closure at 2e-14 per cent and the predicate test are all insensitive to tearing. This is the same class of failure as the conical-region bug, and the same lesson the paper draws about it applies to the paper itself.
manifold_defect_found_and_fixed.THE_FIX: Intersection points are cached per edge in clip_halfspace, so both facets sharing a cut edge reference the same vertex.
manifold_defect_found_and_fixed.a_second_defect_in_the_synthetic_generat: After the fix the synthetic bodies still showed 48 unmatched edges, traced not to the clipper but to synth_bodies: the profile was trimmed at an absolute radius of 1e-12, leaving a ring of vertices at a radius of a few nanometres near each tip, distinct by index but coincident in position. The threshold is now relative, 1e-6 of the maximum half-width. The real shape models were never affected, since they are supplied as meshes.
manifold_defect_found_and_fixed.EFFECT_ON_THE_NUMBERS: The volumes are unchanged to every digit printed, which is expected: the volume never depended on the connectivity. Whether the POTENTIAL changes is a separate question and has to be measured, because the polyhedral gravity evaluation is a sum over facets and may or may not be sensitive to a torn surface. Every run must be repeated.
manifold_defect_found_and_fixed.new_permanent_check: check_manifold() reports repeated directed edges, unmatched directed edges and the Euler characteristic, and now runs on every region and in the self-test. A region that fails is aborted rather than reported.

EFFECT_ON_THE_NUMBERS_MEASURED.test: Itokawa head model at x = 0.1608 km, unreduced mesh, rerun with the corrected clipper and compared against the recorded values
EFFECT_ON_THE_NUMBERS_MEASURED.CONCLUSION: Every reported quantity changes by less than one part in ten thousand of a per cent, and both recovered densities are identical. The results of this paper stand and the full set of runs does not need repeating.
EFFECT_ON_THE_NUMBERS_MEASURED.why_the_potential_was_insensitive: The Werner-Scheeres formulation sums over facets using vertex coordinates directly and never consults connectivity. Two coincident copies of a vertex supply identical coordinates, so the sum is unchanged; the residual movement in the sixth decimal is floating-point summation order. This had to be measured rather than assumed: had any part of the implementation used vertex adjacency, the same defect would have corrupted every result silently.
EFFECT_ON_THE_NUMBERS_MEASURED.status: DEFECT FIXED, RESULTS UNAFFECTED. Report both facts in the paper.

full_rerun_with_corrected_code.UNDECIMATED_RESULTS_UNCHANGED: Itokawa at 49,152 facets (20 models), Eros (2), Arrokoth (5) and all eight synthetic bodies reproduce their recorded values to every printed digit. The clipper corrections therefore do not affect any result taken from a full-resolution mesh.

NEW_FACTS_TO_REPORT: The Arrokoth shape model of Porter et al. (2024) is supplied as two unjoined shells: chi = 4 with two connected components. A region cut beyond the neck is therefore legitimately in two pieces, and a manifold criterion that expects chi = 2 would wrongly reject it. The check used here compares chi against twice the component count.
The 67P SPC 2017 shape model is not a closed surface as supplied: one repeated and two unmatched directed edges. The defect is inherited by any region cut from it.

Vertex clustering does not preserve topology, and the damage grows with the reduction: on a synthetic bilobe a 43% reduction already leaves 96 repeated directed edges, and on 67P a 96% reduction leaves 1,449.
Vertex clustering also ignores the requested target below a certain size, because the grid resolution comes from a fixed ladder. Targets of 1200, 800, 500 and 300 all return the same 2,159-face mesh.

PAPER_IV_RECHECK.STATUS: SUPERSEDED by ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_question. The measurements here stand; the interpretation does not. The conclusion drawn at the time, that the Paper IV claim fails under a better decimator, was wrong on both counts: the decimators are equally accurate, and the Paper IV claim is confirmed by an analytic reference.
PAPER_IV_RECHECK.what_was_done: Mean slope and normalised dispersion recomputed on the four resolution bodies of Paper IV (Eros, Itokawa, Gaspra, Ida) over the ladder 2k to 42k facets, with each decimator, using Paper IV's own surface_fields routine.

dispersion_is_essentially_unchanged.at_the_finest_mesh: the two decimators agree to better than 0.02% on every body
dispersion_is_essentially_unchanged.plateau_between_the_two_finest: 0.000 to 0.098% for both, against the 0.00 to 0.60% reported in Paper IV

SLOPE_IS_NOT.clustering: mean slope rises monotonically with facet count on all four bodies: +21.9%, +14.2%, +5.8%, +1.8%. A coarse clustered mesh reports a systematically lower slope.
SLOPE_IS_NOT.interpretation: the monotonic drift is a decimation artefact. Vertex clustering merges vertices that fall in the same grid cell, which flattens ridges and scarps and lowers the computed slope; quadric collapse is designed to preserve shape and does not.

EFFECT_ON_THE_PAPER_IV_CLAIM.published_claim: the mean slope varies by 1.8 to 25.6% across the mesh ladder while the dispersion varies by only 0.9 to 5.9%, so the dispersion is mesh-convergent where the slope is not
EFFECT_ON_THE_PAPER_IV_CLAIM.conclusion: WITHDRAWN. See ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_question. Judged against an analytic ellipsoid rather than against a finer mesh, the dispersion is 19 to 59 times more accurate than the slope, so the Paper IV claim holds. What this recheck does establish is the narrower point that the NUMERICAL VALUES of a slope statistic depend on the decimation method and should be reported with it.
what_still_stands: The dispersion is stable under refinement: 1.3 to 5.7% over the ladder and below 0.1% between the two finest meshes, on both decimators.
The physical reason: the dispersion is an integral quantity, built from a potential that sums over the whole body, while the slope is local and depends on the orientation of individual facets.
Paper V needs only the first of these, and is unaffected.
EFFECT_ON_THE_PAPER_IV_CLAIM.wider_implication: Any slope statistic reported from a decimated shape model without stating the decimation method may be low by as much as 18%. That is a methodological result of some value in its own right.

PAPER_IV_RECHECK.NOT_YET_SETTLED: Whether quadric collapse is genuinely more accurate, or merely different, is being tested against a homogeneous ellipsoid, whose surface gravity has an exact closed form (MacMillan). That test needs no assumption about which mesh is the truth. Do not act on the Paper IV recheck until it returns.

ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_que.STATUS: AUTHORITATIVE. Supersedes PAPER_IV_RECHECK, which was marked preliminary and is now partly retracted.
ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_que.method: A homogeneous ellipsoid has an exact closed form for its interior and surface gravity (MacMillan 1930): g_i = -2 pi G rho a b c A_i x_i, with A_i an elliptic integral. The area-weighted mean slope and the normalised dispersion then follow by quadrature on the exact surface, owing nothing to any mesh, to the polyhedral code, or to either decimator. Three ellipsoids, three spin states and five facet counts were tested against that reference, ninety configurations in all.
ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_que.formula_verified_against_itself: the sphere limit reproduces GM/R^2 to 2.2e-14 per cent

RESULT_1_the_decimators_are_equivalent_i.reading: Vertex clustering is marginally the more accurate of the two on a smooth surface. The difference is not significant, and neither method is better in the sense of reproducing the truth.

RETRACTION_of_the_earlier_claim.what_was_claimed: That quadric collapse is more accurate than vertex clustering, and that clustering biases the mean slope downward by merging vertices across ridges.
RETRACTION_of_the_earlier_claim.why_it_was_claimed: The four real bodies show a monotonic rise of mean slope with facet count under clustering (+21.9%, +14.2%, +5.8%, +1.8%) and no trend under quadric collapse. With the finest mesh taken as the reference, that reads as a systematic downward bias in the coarse clustered meshes.
RETRACTION_of_the_earlier_claim.what_the_ellipsoid_shows: Neither method carries such a drift. Both overestimate the slope on coarse meshes, by the same amount, and both converge smoothly and monotonically toward the analytic value as the mesh refines. The signed error is positive in all ninety configurations for both methods.
RETRACTION_of_the_earlier_claim.status: RETRACTED. The claim that quadric collapse is more accurate is withdrawn, as is the ridge-merging explanation.

ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_que.what_remains_unexplained: The monotonic drift under clustering on the four real bodies is real and is not reproduced on a smooth ellipsoid. The natural reading is that it arises from surface roughness, which an ellipsoid does not have, but that is a hypothesis and not a measurement: no analytic reference exists for a rough body, so which decimator is closer to the truth there cannot presently be established.

RESULT_2_PAPER_IV_IS_CONFIRMED_AND_UNDER.reading: Measured against an analytic reference rather than against a finer mesh, the normalised dispersion is 19 to 59 times more accurate than the mean slope at the same facet count. Paper IV inferred a ratio of roughly 3 to 14 from mesh-to-mesh variation, so its central claim is not merely upheld but understated.
RESULT_2_PAPER_IV_IS_CONFIRMED_AND_UNDER.significance: This is a stronger form of the Paper IV result, because it does not assume that the finest mesh is the truth. The dispersion is an integral over the whole body and the slope is local; the ellipsoid puts a number on how much that matters.

CONSEQUENCES: Paper IV does not need a corrected version. Its conclusion holds and is conservative.
Paper V should report the ellipsoid test as an independent confirmation of the Paper IV result, not as a correction of it.

Quadric collapse remains the decimator of choice, but for topology rather than accuracy: it preserves the manifold property, which is required for any later work needing vertex normals or inward offsetting, and it returns the requested facet count exactly, which clustering does not.
Papers III and IV used vertex clustering, and nothing in this test invalidates the numbers they report.
ellipsoid_test_settles_the_decimator_que.limitation_of_this_test: An ellipsoid is smooth. Real bodies are not, and the one effect that distinguishes the two decimators on real bodies is precisely the one an ellipsoid cannot exhibit. The test settles the question of accuracy on smooth surfaces and leaves the rough case open.
